FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 97) respecting Insurance. He said: Mr., Speaker: This Bill is to a very large extent the Bill which was presented to the House last session and held over for further consideration. It is not, however, the same in all respects. The Bill of last year was the subject of a protracted hearing and inquiry before the committee on Banking and Commerce, during which many suggestions were offered by way of amendment. We have had the benefit of that inquiry, and the benefit of the further study which has been had of the Bill in consequence of the delay; and with the better light which has come to us we have endeavoured to make some improvements in the Bill. I shall call the attention of the House to the points in which, the Bill differs materially from that of last year. We do not make any change in the existing law with respect to the assessment insurance companies. A proposal in relation to these institutions was made in the Bill of last year; but even if we had gone on with that Bill, that proposal, as was stated; at the time, would have been withdrawn.
The principal companies engaged in that line of business represented to us that they recognized the necessity for strengthening their position, that they were going about it in their own way and desired to be left to themselves for that purpose. We are aware that efforts are being made in that direction and so we do not propose in this Bill to make any change in the existing law with respect to these organizations. Probably the question of investments is the one which engaged the most attention before the committee last year We have made some changes with respect to the provisions on that subject to which I shall invite the attention of the House. Section 60 of the new Bill will read:
Any life insurance company which derives its corporate powers, or any of them, from an Act of the parliament of Canada, or which is within the legislative power of the parliament of Canada, may invest its funds, or any portion thereof, in the purchase of-
(a) The debentures, bonds, stocks, or other securities of or guaranteed by the government of the Dominion of Canada, or of or guaranteed by the government of the United Kingdom, or of any colony or dependency thereof, or of or guaranteed by the government of any foreign country, or state forming a portion of such foreign country, wherein the company carries on or is about to carry on business, provided the Treasury Board has signified its approval of such securities, or of any municipal or school corporation in Canada, or elsewhere where the company is carrying on business.
That is substantially the same as in the Bill of last year.
Subsection (b) 1 includes among the securities in which a company may invest
The bonds of any company which bonds are secured by a mortgage to trustees or a trust corporation, or otherwise, upon real estate or other assets of such company.
The former Bill required that these bonds should be outstanding for at least five years. In the present Bill we have dropped the time condition; if the bonds are secured by mortgage they are deemed to be good and may be used as a field for investment. The former Bill restricted these bonds to the bonds of a corporation incorporated in a country in which the insurance company v as carrying on business. We have, after the discussion which has taken place, removed that restriction. Subsection 2 of subsection (b) reads:
The debentures or other evidences of indebtedness of any Company, which has been doing business for a term of not less than five years prior to the date of such investments, provided default shall not have been made by such company in the interest payments upon its debentures or other evidences of indebtedness within the said period of five years prior to such investment.
In the former Bill it was required that such debentures should be of seven years' standing. In the present Bill we apply the time limit not to the debentures but to the standing of the company which issues the debentures. If a company is of five years' standing and has made no default it is presumed that its debentures may be treated as good.
Subsection 3 of subsection (b) reads:
The preferred or guaranteed stocks of any company which has paid regular dividends upon such stocks or upon its common stocks for not less than five years preceding the purchase of such preferred or guaranteed stocks.
Last year's Bill provided that such stocks should have paid 4 per cent for seven years. The present year drops the 4 per cent condition and provides that the company shall have paid regular dividends for five years on this class of stock but does not specify the rate. The argument is that this is a high class of stock which may in some instances not pay as much as 4 per cent, and that it is not wise to insist upon the 4 per cent rate.
Subsection 4 of subsection (b) reads:
The common stocks of any such company upon which regular dividends of at least 4 per cent have been paid for the seven years next preceding the purchase of such stocks: Provided that not more than 20 per cent of the common stocks and not more than 20 per cent of the total issue of the stocks of any company shall be purchased by any such life insurance company, and that no company shall be permitted to invest in its own shares

or in the shares of another life insurance company.
Last year's Bill provided that the common stock should have paid at least five per cent dividends for ten years. The present Bill recognizes the stock as good if it has paid four per cent for seven years.
There is a proviso here as to the percentage of money which may be invested in the securities of any one company. The object of that was to provide that the company should not create a subsidiary company and obtain a controlling interest in it. It was found, however, that the words of the clause seemed to be too broad, and we have now amended it. Last year's Bill limited the investment to twenty per cent of all the stocks or securities of the company. In the present Bill we are distinguishing between the stocks and bonds and our proviso is that the investment may not exceed twenty per cent of the sto'cks of any company, but we leave the company free to invest in the bonds if they are deemed to be good security.
Subsections (c) and (d) of this clause recognize ground rents or mortgages on real estate, and life and endowment policies as proper subjects for investment, but these are not changes and it is not necessary to say anything concerning them.
A question arose as to what action should be taken respecting any investments of a company in securities which might not come within the new law. Provision was made that in the case of securities not recognized by the new Bill the securities should be disposed of within a certain time. We have changed that to provide that where the investments were made in securities which at the time of their purchase were legal and proper the company shall be free to dispose of them at such time as it may find most convenient. In the case of securities which, at the time of their purchase were not strictly within the terms of the old Insurance Act-this applies in one or two instances-provision is made that such securities shall be disposed of within a period of five years.
A question which has received great attention in the discussion of insurance matters is the expenses of management. In the last Bill provision was made for a limitation of the expense on new business, and at one stage it seemed that such a rovision was called for, if not by what ad occurred in Canada by the developments in other countries. In the investigations abroad great importance was attached to this question but when it came to be discussed with insurance men here before the committee it was urged that it would be exceedingly difficult to apply a limitation of that kind without interfering with the volume of insurance. It was held that the proposed limitation would so hamper the insurance agents that they

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
would not be able to make a respectable income and would not enter the field, so that there would be a falling off in the amount of insurance, which is not desirable, because we all feel that the encouragement of life insurance is a good thing. We have inserted a provision in the present Bill not to put any limitation on the expense of new business particularly but to provide a limitation upon the expenses generally. If this proviso were not qualified, it might prove a great handicap to new companies. The expenses of management of a new company are necessarily greater in proportion than the expenses of an old company with a large volume of business, so we propose that the limitation of expenses shall apply to old companies which have a standing of fifteen years, or to any company so soon as it comes to the age of fifteen years, and that in the case of new companies to be incorporated hereafter, this limitation shall begin when they have had ten years of existence. Last year's Bill required that the returns should show the expense of new business separate from ordinary business. Such a division has been found difficult and we have dropped this provision and substituted one providing for a return of what is technically called a gain and loss exhibit which it is thought might to some extent serve the same purpose. Last year's Bill proposed that each class of insurance should be dealt with in a separate policy.
This year's Bill continues that provision, with, however, this qualification,-that accident and sickness insurance may be deemed as practically one, and these two may be included in one policy.
There is a provision with regard to what I may call the exchange of securities; that is to say where a company is required by the terms of the proposed legislation to dispose of securities within a given time, it may be found convenient that they should exchange these securities for some others which, while not coming within the class approved by the Bill, would still be desirable securities and of a better class than those now held by the company. The conditions are somewhat exceptional, and we think it well to make a provision which will meet those conditions.
There is a provision that no life insurance company shall loan any of its funds to any director, shareholder, officer or clerk thereof. That should not be held to interfere with the ordinary loan to any policy-holder who is entitled to receive it, merely because he is an officer of the company. Possibly this clause needs to be made a little clearer on that point.
With regard to the election of directors by the shareholders and the policy-holders, some of the companies now provide for policy-holders' directors. It is proposed that there shall be a general law in that

respect, and that all life insurance companies, shall provide for their policy-holders, as well as for their shareholders, having directors. It was represented to us before the committee that a few people might possibly acquire the power of directors and bring about hasty, radical changes in the management, a thing that certainly would not be desirable. To guard against this, it is proposed to provide that a certain number shall retire annually, so that there shall not be, at any time, a radical change in the directorate.
What is the proportion of policy-holders' directors?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The same number of each; policy-holders and shareholders have an equal number of directors, and two of each class retire every year. In the Bill of last year it was provided that proxies should be recognized. This is continued, with the proviso that proxies shall not be good for more than three months.
Will a shareholder be eligible as a policy-holders' director?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, every director must he chosen from his own class.
But a shareholder may be also a policy-holder. What I desire to ask is whether a shareholder will be eligible as a policy-holders' director? No shareholder should be eligible for that position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is the provision of the Bill. Provision is made that a company may withdraw itself from Dominion jurisdiction. A case has arisen recently of a company that has a Dominion license, but wishes to confine its business to one province only, and so desires to withdraw its Dominion deposit and have it transferred to the Insurance Department of the province. There seems to be no objection to such a procedure, but we have no machinery in the Insurance Act to deal with it, and we propose to insert a clause granting that power.
Now, a question that was brought to the notice of the committee last year is that of publicity. It was urged by the representatives of the companies that some of the restrictions proposed to be placed upon them were not necessary, but that the best guarantee the public could have was adequate publicity. One of the features we inserted in the Bill was that the returns should show the sums received by any officer or agent of the company in excess of a moderate amount-that is, in excess of $4,000. It was presumed that the ordinary life insurance agent, the great bulk of them, would receive less than that amount, and that, though a limited number might receive a larger sum, there would not be any
trouble in providing a return .of that character. It is but fair to say that we were not aware of any serious difficulty having occurred in Canada in relation to that point, though it is well known that one of the abuses shown up in the investigation in the United States was that very large sums were paid to officers of the company. Our contention is that if any such large sum be paid for good and sufficient reason, the public should be made aware of the fact through the return. It was, however, pointed out to us that such a return, when made public, might be misleading, inasmuch as many of the insurance agents have to pay their subagents, and therefore the amounts that might be placed opposite their names would not represent their own earnings, but only money that had passed through their hands. We continue the clause in the Bill, with the proviso, however, that, wherever the agent referred to us in receipt of money which he has in part to pay to subagents, that shall be indicated by a remark in the return, so that those who read will be made aware that the amount received by the agent is not entirely for himself.
A change is made in the tables used for the valuation of policies. The table in use for many years was what is known as the Hm. table of the Institute of Actuaries of Great Britain. A more modern table is the British Offices Life Table which has come into more general use. It is proposed to adopt this table.
We have added another part to the Bill, part 5, for the purpose of including in the Act a number of the clauses which are to he found in the Companies' Clauses Act, which, as hon. members who have had experience in the Banking and Commerce Committee know, are frequently referred to, a common provision in a private Bill being that such and such clauses of the Companies' Clauses Act shall apply and others shall not apply. That is often confusing. We propose to import into this Bill all the clauses of the Companies' Clauses^ Act that are useful for the purposes of insurance companies. We have added a form of model Bill, which it is hoped will be adopted, and will facilitiate the insurance legislation of the future. So many things have been carried into the charters of companies that sometimes they become embarrassing. We have thought it best that everything should be gathered into one Bill, and then a company's charter should be, as bank charters are, a simple measure.
The Bill is a somewhat lengthy one, com-pi ising, including the schedule, 94 pages. It is to be remembered, however, that it is not quite so ponderous as it seems, for the bulk of it is merely a consolidation of the existing law.
I propose, at an early day, after the Bill is in the hands of hon. members-as it will

be immediately-to move the second reading and ask that the Bill be referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce. It has been suggested by an hon. member who is much interested in this measure, that we could effectively deal with it by 'appointing a small sub-committee of the Banking and Commerce Committee to consider it. That ccmmends itself to my judgment, but the motion for that purpose would have to be made in the Committee on Banking and C< mmerce itself.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 98) to amend the Exchequer Court Act. He said: The purpose of this Bill is simply to make the Civil Service Amendment Act, which was passed last session, apply to the registrar of the Exchequer Court. It is probable that such was the intention when the Act of last session was passed. The status and the salary of the registrar are fixed by special Act, and his position not being mentioned specially in the Act amending the Civil Service Act the special Act would still continue to apply to him, unless we pass legislation of the character I am introducing.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

CONMEE (Thunder Bay) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 99) to amend the Railway Act. He said: The object is to amend the Act in respect of the maintenance of fences and cattle guards in certain sections where, under the present law, the onus is thrown entirely upon the settler. If his land is inclosed and .an accident occurs he may recover damages, but if his land is not inclosed, damages cannot be recovered. Parliament must have intended the law to work a little differently, but that seems to be the effect, and my information is that the courts have held that such is the case. That is a matter which ought to be remedied.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

About a year ago the freight clerks in Halifax and St. Johns had some difficulty with the Intercolonial Railway management. After some little time, it was decided to refer the matter to arbitration under the conciliation clause of the Act known as the Lemieux Act. There was a board of arbitration Mr. FIELDING.
which sat in Halifax and in Ottawa during the summer, and whose finding, I understood, was in favour of the clerks. But nothing has since been heard of it and no settlement has been made. I would like to know why the finding of that arbitration has not been carried out.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: It is very doubtful whether the finding is in favour of the clerks or not. It is the finding to which my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) referred previously, and it has been referred to in questions and answers several times since. That finding in brief was to the effect that the number of the clerks could be diminished and the salary of the remainder increased without increasing the expenditure of the railway in that connection. _ If it had been simply a question of increasing the salaries, there would have been no difficulty, but there is also question of depriving several men of their employment, and the department had to ascertain all the information possible, as to the dates of the appointments of these men, their salaries and ability as clerks. That work is not yet completed. As soon as we can get the full information, we shall make up our minds.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

speechtext:
House in committee on Bill (No. 29) respecting the Winnipeg and North Western Railway Company.-Mr. McCraney.
On section 1:

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
I have just a word to say in regard to this Bill. If you will permit me to digress just for the space of one minute I will give you the reason why I was not here when the Bill was before the House on Friday last. I was at that time in what is called room 89, the room set aside for the Conservative members, in committee considering a proper change of name for that room and on which the committee came to the decision that perhaps it would be well to call it the Saragossa Sea. The reason of that was because, like the Sea of Saragossa, all the relics, wreckage, debris, flotsam and jetsam are gathered there. I would point out to the minister who is in charge of the furnishing of that room that it would be well that he should send these ancient relics of the time of Alexander Mackenzie to a museum instead of leaving them there for the use of members. There are fourteen kinds of chairs hardly a table with four legs and I think this is very unfair treatment to be accorded to the loyal opposition in this House.
With regard to this Bill, I will say a few words which will not only be my words but which will voice the opinions of the people whom I have the honour to represent. This charter has been objected to by every municipality through which this proposed railway is projected to run. The objections were taken in the proper way, through the municipal officers and by petition to the government, copies of which petitions were sent to me. I will read you. sir, because I want in ' Hansard,' what one of these petitions sets forth:
Whereas, the Winnipeg and North Western Railway Company have given notice of intention to apply at the next session of the parliament of Canada for an Act extending the time for the construction and completion of this railway;	. .	...	.	_
And whereas the municipality of bte. Rose is interested in the matter;
(This happens to be the petition of Ste. Rose in Ochre river, Dauphin, Gilbert Plains, Grand View and Shell River; all the municipalities concerned, are associated with this petition).
And whereas the speedy construction and completion of a railway along the proposed route will he a great he no lit to the people of this district;	.
And whereas the speedy construction and completion of such a railway is desirable;
And whereas, the privilege that has from time to time been granted to railways through-

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: How did the other men vote; on party lines too?

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I beg your pardon, Sir, you were not there and you are not in a position to know. Unfortunately for my presentation of the case before the committee some of my Conservative friends voted against me, but all the Liberals voted solid also against me. It is a great mistake that partyism should be allowed to enter into the affairs of that committee. Later on, when I saw that this amendment which I had the committee insert for the benefit of the people and at their request, was to be cut out, I did not want to waste the time of the committee and I had to accept my defeat as gracefully as I could, but that does not prevent me from saying a few words here. I had put in this amendment that the company be compelled to Mr. CAMPBELL.
build 25 miles in the first year in order to show its bona fides. The promoters of the road had said through their solicitor that they had the money and that they were willing to complete the road in five years and considering that they were chartered to build from 1,500 to 2,000 miles and that they undertook to complete that in five years, surely it was not a hardship on them to ask that they should build at least 25 miles in the first year.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: How long had they the charter?

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: For two years. I wish now to enter my protest. There is hardly a member from the west who does not express the opinion in private conversation that something ought to be done to compel these hot air lines to either get out of business and let some one get into business or compel them to show their bona fides right away. The only argument put up by gentlemen on the other side is that it has been customary to allow this, but if in the past we have done wrong is it not time to make a change and let us do right now?

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: At the first meeting of the Railway Committee at which this Bill was discussed it was stated that certain petitions had been sent to the government, and it was intimated that the government had taken no action in the matter. The deputy minister who was present, stated that no petitions had been received, and subsequently it turned out that the petitions referred to my hon. friend from Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) did not go to the Department of Railways and Canals, but to the Board of Railway Commissioners, so that these petitions had never been before the Department of Railways and Canals. They were, however, before the committee when the Bill was finally considered and passed upon.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
That is rather important. The hon. member for Dauphin stated in the committee that petitions had been sent in and that it was the duty of the Minister of Railways to acquaint the committee of any petitions that had been received against the passage of the Act. It now appears that the Railway Board received these petitions instead of the minister, and I venture to say it was the duty of the Railway Board to forward these petitions to the proper authorities. No one could be in any doubt as to what the proper distinction is for petitions of that kind and no one could doubt the importance of the committee being acquainted with such petitions before we proceed to deal with a Bill of this kind. Of course, in this particular instance, no hardship has occurred, because the hon. member for Dauphin reminds me that he read a copy of the peti-

tion at the time; but it is well to have impressed upon whoever is responsible for the matter in the Railway Board that it would be regarded as their duty to forward these petitions promptly when they come in.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
As one who took an interest in this matter before the committee, I agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Dauphin with regard to the desirability of having some clause to protect ihe people of that district. When this Bill was before the committee, I supported that clause, but I am surprised to find that the Bill was brought back for consideration. I agreed to the compromise that was made on the strength of the statement by the gentleman promoting the Bill, and I think by the chairman of the committee, that a charter over the same route would be granted to any other person applying for it. As a member from the west, I do not feel that I ought to say one word that would make it hard for a promoter to obtain a charter if he means to build the road; but knowing what has occurred in the past, I feel that we have had too many charters that have tied up the district for years and prevented the people getting a much needed road. I notice in the railway committee that a great many gentlemen voted for the reconsideration of the Bill who practically knew nothing at all about it or about the district through which the road was to run or the hardships of the people. If what my hon. friend from Dauphin has said is correct, and it is admitted by the chairman of the Railway Committee that petitions have come in from every municipality of that district asking the government and their representatives to protect their interests, then I feel that the committee has been a little hasty in dealing with the Bill as they have. With the understanding of the committee that the promoters were prepared to complete the road in five years, it is not too much to ask that the people of the district should have some guarantee that they mean business, and I confess frankly that I was a little surprised that there were not more members of the committee who felt as I did. I feel that we have been too liberal in the past in granting railway charters-that we have not tried in any way to restrict the promoters and to make them go on with the work of construction. I think a clause should be put in every charter requiring the promoters to build a certain number of miles each year or to put up fifteen or twenty-five per cent of the cost of the railway as a guarantee. A Bill of that kind is proposed by one of the members from the west, and when it comes before the House, I shall have much pleasure in supporting it. But I think _ the committee were hasty in rushing this Bill through
in the manner they did without taking into consideration all these petitions from the people directly interested.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: 'The speeches which have been made by my hon. friend from Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) and my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) indicate a point of view which we hear discussed very much at meetings of the Railway Committee. What the people of Dauphin are after is to have railways constructed. How are we to get that done? Is it by stopping railways, or is it by helping them? I know that there is a very prevalent opinion throughout this country that- a railway charter is a special privilege, giving an exclusive right to a corporation to build a railway from one point to another. I think that parliament can do a great deal to disabuse the minds of the public on that point. When I first came here I largely shared that view; but from my experience in this House, I have come to the conclusion that parliament does not give exclusive rights. The only right it gives is the right to go on and build, and anybody else who comes to this parliament can acquire the same right, and the right is only vested when the plans are approved of by the Minister of Railways.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Would they get the right over the same route?

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I should say that there is no reason why any company should not be given the right to build a railway from any one point to any other point.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman mean that if anybody else asked for a charter for a railway running over the same route that this railway runs over, he would be able to obtain such a charter?

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I can only speak as a member of this House; but my own attitude would be to support such a measure.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: What does the minister say?

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: There is also a prevalent idea that when a company is given a charter which permits it to build a railway from one point to another point, it is enter ing into a contract with the government to build; that it is in the position of contractors with the government for any other public work, and that when it comes here asking for an extension of time, it should be treated as any other government contractor. The point is altogether left out of consideration that the government is not supplying the money for the work, and therefore parliament cannot force the company to build where it does not want to build.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman states that a franchise of this kind is not a special privilege. I want to ask him if it is not often a very valuable privilege, and one that is sold.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: It is a special privilege, but not an exclusive privilege. It is not a privilege which is refused to any person who comes here and asks for similar legislation. My hon. friend asks: Is this not a right which is sometimes sold-is there not speculation in charters? Perhaps there has been in the past. I would like to see the policy laid down by this parliament of granting charters so freely that there would not be any value in a railway charter except perhaps the value that any railway might have because a certain amount of money has been expended to solicitors and others in getting the legislation through parliament. It is only by having parliament grant unrestricted charters that we can deprive charters of their value. The only way in which the government or parliament can compel the building of railways is to supply the money, but that means government ownership, and I do not think that is a subject for discussion upon this occasion. We have had discussion in this House with reference to paper charters. There is talk of the country being blanketed with charters, talk that one hears perhaps with regard to claims on coal areas or something of that kind, as though when a certain territory is shown as having a railway chartered to go into it, no one else could enter it. If this discussion has only one result, to disabuse the public mind of that idea, it will be justified.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Could the hon. member state just what the practice in reference to that is, I think it is just as well we should understand it. Suppose a charter is given to certain promoters for a railway between two given points. They are allowed by the terms of their charter a certain period within which to commence and a certain other period within which to complete the construction of their line. Every one understands, of course, that there is no technical reason why parliament should not give exactly the same kind of charter to another set of promoters, but in actual practice does the Railway Committee do that ?

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: No, never.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I am not an old enough member of this House to say what the practice has been.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Nor any one else.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: My hon. friend is hardly in a position to say that. Since I have been a member, for the last four

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: years, I am not aware of any charter having been refused for a line which has already been granted by Act of parliament.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Have any been granted ?

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Does the hon. member say that any charter has been granted to a second company for exactly the same line for which charter has been granted to the first company ?

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Generally, practically the same ground.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I would like the hon. member to mention any. It has never been
done.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
It has also been said that because a railway is chartered from one point to another, maps are got out by speculators and settlers are induced to go into the district and establish their homesteads along the proposed line of railway. I must say that in my own riding I have never had to deal with any case of that kind. The only case I know of is that of the Canadian Pacific Railway which in 1907 got a charter for a line from Moosejaw to Lacombe. They advertised for tenders and on the strength of what they had undertaken to do settlers did go out into the country and did settle, then they abandoned what work they had done, they did not go on with their tendering and there certainly was a great protest from my own portion of the country and from the Moosejaw district. Many farmers felt that if they had to go to the next winter without the facilities of a railway and the means of bringing in fuel there might be a great deal of distress.
But it is a different case altogether when a railway like the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian Northern or the Grand Trunk Pacific, all of which are railways of standing in this country and all of which have had assistance from parliament, give assurances and undertake a work, because people expect that that work will be done. I must say that in my own part of the country we have never been misguided because some body obtained a charter for a railway from one part of the country to another. If we in this parliament should make the restriction pro posed, we would make it possible only for those who can meet the conditions placed upon the corporations to build railways, and that would prevent any new corporation from going into the railway business in this country. I think there is a very general impression throughout the country that it is the common stockholders who build roads and perhaps this parliament may disabuse the public mind of that idea also; we will learn that it is not the common stockholders that build railroads but

the bondholders who negotiate for the construction on terms favourable not to the government or to the population to be served by the railroad but to themselves. That is the only way in which money for these undertakings can be raised. This particular case is one of the best cases to bring before this House because it is an extreme case and because the principle can best be discussed in view of the fact that this company has been incorporated for less than two years. I think my hon. friend stated too strongly what the promoters of the Bill said in the Railway Committee. My recollection was not that the promoter of the Bill who appeared before the Railway Committee said that they have the means in hand to go on with this; what he did say was that they were doing their very best to get the money.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I think he said it was in sight

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
He said they expected to get it, but he gave no assurance that the money had been secured. What would be the position of affairs if the restriction desired by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) were imposed? If the bonds were floated and if less than twenty-five miles were built in one year what would happen? I am sure the bondholders would feel very insecure, and with that prospect in sight would be very unwilling indeed to invest their money in this enterprise.
I have been discussing the case of m\ hon. friend's constituency. I have a paper before me now which I received this morning and which gives a case in my own constituency which well illustrates 'the point. I have here the minutes of the Fertile Valley Liberal Association. I shall read one resolution:

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Stephens moved and was seconded by iMr. G. H. McKague, that the Association place before the government an objection to an extension of time to the Canadian Pacific Railway for the completion of their Moosejaw-Lacombe line; that they recommend the government to refuse to grant such extensions and that W. Kennedy and the secretary draft a protest and ask Mr. Knowles and Mr. Mc-Craney to take up the matter with the government and the Railway Commission. Carried unanimously.
The Liberal Association of Fertile Valley want to accomplish the same result as do the friends of the hon. member for Dauphin, they want to get the railway and they want me to do what my hon. friend's, friends want him to do, to secure a refusal of the extension of time except on conditions. A year ago the Canadian Pacific Railway declined to go on with this very road and at the last session this House voted $3,200 a mile for this extension to a distance of 123 miles. That was the reason the road was built, it was not because they
had a charter. As a matter of fact I think that the Canadian Pacific Railway did not' want to build the road, that they had concluded that, for some time at least, the traffic in that particular part of the country would not warrant its construction. The reason the road was built was because this parliament voted $3,200 per mile. To my mind the way to get this road built is not to refuse an extension of time but to help the railway company. That is to be my answer to my own constituents who want me, in this and other cases, to refuse the extension of time. If there is anything this government can do to help the railways by assisting them financially, that is what I would support, and I would support it with reference to my hon. friend's constituency as well as with reference to my own. I think that is the only way in which this question can be dealt with, and that we should accomplish nothing by putting restrictions upon the applications for charters which come before this House.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The hon. member (Mr. McCraney) has not met the question quite squarely. Nobody has proposed to refuse this company an extension of time. The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) was as urgent in desiring that this company should have an extension of time as any other member of the committee. But he desired that the people should be served by a railway, and so he proposed that conditions should be provided which he thought reasonable and in the public interest to bring about the construction of the road. He succeeded in convincing the committee at its first sitting that he was right, and his amendment was carried. But a majority of the committee saw fit to reconsider the question and proposed the modification which, as I recollect, was not proposed at the first meeting but which is in harmony with our general practice. I hope the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCraney) does not wish it to go abroad, or to be suggested in this House, that the hon. member for Dauphin, or any other member of the committee, refused this company a reasonable extension of time. What the hon. member for Dauphin and those who supported him voted for was that the company should have a reasonable time to carry out their undertaking, having regard to the statement made that they had money ready to carry on their work. The hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. McCraney) spoke as if he was going to tell something of the inner life of the Railway Committee, which, I think, it might be well to have told in this House. But as to this question of paralleling lines, we need hardly discuss it, because it is not the policy of this parliament. When the Transcontinental line was under discussion, we were emphatic in saying that we did not want parallel lines, and ought to

keep every railway a certain distance from another. In fact, I should not be surprised if, in the statute-book, we had a provision that lines should not approach each other closer than within certain limits.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Was not that in reference to construction lines?

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: We would not grant a charter to parallel an existing line except at a certain distance.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That is a line already built.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Yes, but the policy of parliament is that it is better to have one line of railway with large traffic than two struggling for existence, each with a small traffic. For that reason it would be unwise for us to grant a charter to parallel a line for which a charter had already been granted. It would be absurd to expect the Minister of Railways or any other responsible adviser of the Crown to sanction the granting of a charter to a new company to build over practically the same ground the right to build over which had already been granted to an existing company. We do not do it, and we would not do it. In spite of what the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) says, I venture to say he cannot find an instance where we have granted a charter to cover ground already covered to a company that is not in default. The people have to pay the freight rates, and the Board of Railway Commissioners will fix those rates according to the traffic. If you divide the traffic by two, and then divide it by two again, making four lines where there is traffic for only one, you increase the burdens of the people, and it is folly to say that when we grant a charter to such a company as this with three or four alternative routes we do not cover that country and prevent other companies coming in to build so long as that charter exists. The consequence is that the company that has obtained a charter has a franchise which can be sold in the market. The proof is that it has been done over and over again and is being done all the time. We have no objection to a renewal of the charter, but we do object to their obtaining it on terms not in the interests of the public.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
If there is any impression that the Railway Committee refuses to grant charters because charters have been granted over the same ground, I can only say that it is a very erroneous impression. In the past five years I have never known a charter to be refused by a railway company^ because a charter had already been issued. But I may point out to my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) Mr. LENNOX.
that not only does the Railway Committee and this House, grant such charters, but the Railway Department has, in several cases, approved the plans and allowed the railways to build, paralleling .each other over the same ground. You have only to look at the map of the country west of Winnipeg-I do not at this moment speak of the eastern portion of Canada-and you will (find railway after tailway running arallel to another for miles. West of askatoon, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Pacific parallel each other within a stone's throw. West of Edmonton, the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific run parallel to each other for over a hundred miles, practically on the same territory. In my own constituency the Canadian Pacific Railway branch lines parallel each other for nearly 80 miles. I vcted against the amendment of the hon. member for Dauphin, and did so because this is the first time that this company has come before parliament asking for an extension of time. And it is not altogether asking an extension of time, because in its application it asks for a charter covering two or three other branch lines that it had not before ; so_ that, to some extent, it is a new application altogether. And we we were assured by the representatives of the company that they were in a fair way to get the money to build the road next year, but if that clause was put in this year, it would prevent them getting the money, and so prevent their going on. This road is chartered among a number of existing branches of the Canadian Northern. I do not know how it is in this case, but I know that in other cases, railway companies have engineered just such petitions as have come in here, and if we had knocked this charter out, the effect would have been to leave that company with absolute control of all the roads in that part of the country. I agree with my hon. friend from Dauphin that a railway company should be made to build each year, but I claim that this should apply to every railway company and not to one in particular-not to pick out and penalize one company. I trust that when I get my Bill, now on the Order Paper, to the right point, I should receive the general support of both sides. The Bill would make it incumbent on all these railway companies to build at least twenty-five miles in the first two years-that is if the road chartered is less than 250 miles long-then in the third and fourth years an additional twenty-five miles each, and complete in five years, and, if they do not do this, they will be compelled to come back to this House and get an extension of time.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman made the statement that it has not been the practise of the Railway Committee to duplicate charters from one given point to another,

and he gave us an illustration in the Grand Trunk Pacific. But every one knows that the Grand Trunk Pacific was given a special charter with special conditions and with a distinct promise to the country that it would not parallel any existing line but be a great colonization road. We learn now, however, that it is simply a parallel line to two or three others and is not serving the purpose for which it was intended.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I want to say a few words on this matter because I have given a good deal of attention to what goes on in the Railway Committee. If the right hon. gentleman who leads the House could occasionally give enough time to visit that committee, he would see that there is an absolute need for reform. Every hon. gentleman who is on that committee knows that every day a considerable percentage of its members sit at the far end of the room swap stories with one another and pay no attention whatever to the subject before the committee. Then when the gentleman who has charge of the Bill-especially if he happens to be a government whip-stands up, they vote straight every time. I do not think there is an hon. gentleman on either side who will contradict me.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Do you say they vote straight?

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
They vote according to the wishes of the promoter of the Bill without considering anything else. The hon. gentleman who introduced this Bill seems to think that there can be no harm even if you do give several charters in the same district. He would advocate free trade in railways and let every company be incorporated and build if it pleases. But anybody, who has any practical knowledge of the methods of getting money to construct such works, will know that there could be no more effective way to prevent capital being invested in railway construction in the northwest. What the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Glen Campbell) said in the committee is perfectly right. He said he had no desire to obstruct the particular company referred to in the Bill and he wanted to see the railway built, but he wanted to get rid of hot air companies, and he argued that if the company in question professes to be able to construct 1,500 miles of railway in five years, it surely will be able to construct 25 miles in one, and he proposed to put that in the Bill.
The counsel who was there representing the directors said they had been endeavouring to get the companies floated in Paris or London but had not been able owing to the financial crisis. Now, however, they thought they were in the way of getting it placed and were confident they could do so. Any one who saw the project laid out on the map like a great spider, with its arms projecting in all directions
over some 1,500 miles of railway, would see that instead of that company assisting in a construction of railways in that district, it would have the opposite effect. If any other people wanted to take any section of that territory and build 500 or 200 miles of railway, they would be met at once by the fact that these people had mapped out the whole district and covered it with projected branches in all directions, so that no one would advance a cent for other lines. That is just where hot air companies, by holding up their territory from year to year, can delay the construction of a railway in every inch of the territory thus covered. For that -qo o^ po^uim eq osneooq iou pun uosum struct or delay-he wants just the opposite -the hon. member for Dauphin objected to these charters being renewed as a matter of course. One gentleman will say, what is the harm ? They have only applied once or twice. Their charter perhaps was given some ten years ago, and not a dollar has since been expended, yet they remain quite confident they can build the road. Any one who sees what is going on knows that as long as such charters are renewed, so long will they cherish the hope of making something out of it, and while there is the remotest chance of their doing so, they will apply for a renewal.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) is quite) fair in the reference he made to the committee. It is true that many of the members of the committee do not take a very active part in its work, but that is the case with all committees. The same may be said of this House. A great many members do not take part in any of the debates and a very limited number only take part in the debates upon general subjects, but I do not think that would warrant any one saying that the members of one political party merely followed their leader. I do not think that is more true of the Liberals than of the Conservatives, because I know of several Bills in regard to which the members of the Conservative party in the Railway Committee were lined up on certain occasions and followed their leaders very closely. But I am not prepared to say that the Conservatives voted for party purposes. I do not think that the hon. member for Dauphin really meant that the Liberals who voted against his view did so for party purposes, because if that were true his own Conservative friends were removed by similar motives. I wish to say that we canot build railways by legislation. If by an Act of parliament we could cause a railway to be constructed in this or that direction, but that we cannot do. There are occasions, when, if restrictions are put on railway charters which are promoted by individuals, you hamper these individuals and defeat the very purpose you have in view.

The hon. member for Dauphin expressed the opinion that if a company were compelled to build a certain number of miles during a certain number of years, that would bring about more rapid construction of railways.
I am quite satisfied that the reverse would be the case. I know of more than one railway undertaking that has been wrecked by premature expenditure. Take this case. I do not know the local conditions ; therefore I am not going to speak as if I did, but I will ask my hon. friend to assume this condition of things:	Suppose
they build twenty-five miles and there is no traffic there would be perhaps nearly a million of money expended. If there is no traffic, the undertaking is not successful, there is no good purpose served by the expenditure of the money that is invested. What good is that going to do anybody ? That does not do the country any good and it embarrasses the company because they are not in the same position to go into the money market and obtain capital. The hen. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) stated that nothing would embarrass a company more than the granting of a charter in the vicinity of this line. I cannot agree with him. Nothing will help the company more. It will give the investing public knowledge that that section of the country is important when some other company wants to build a line of railway. It is just a case of the survival of the fittest. Let those build who can build. If you put restrictions upon the charter, if you take away the opportunity from one set of men who have perhaps spent a great deal of money and devoted a great deal of energy and time to the undertaking to proceed with the work you are not advancing the construction of the railway. The reasonable thing would be to give to any others who wish it the opportunity to build the road. If they have the capital, or if they can procure it more quickly then, they will build the road. There will not be two lines built. Our country has not yet got into that condition where our railways are injured by competing lines. I can remember-and I will not admit that I am very old yet-when the Grand Trunk thought they were the objects of a severe attack because it was proposed to build another line between Montreal and Toronto. The line was built and it did the Grand Trunk good. The prosperity of the country was increased. These railways bring traffic; they do not take traffic away from each other, except at competitive points. It is just so in other sections of the country.'' The hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) says that we do not grant charters to lines paralleling other lines. We are doing it every day. There has been hardly a year in the last four or five years but what, for fifty miles or a hundred Mr. CONMEE.
miles, or in some cases, for the entire length of the line, charters have been given practically in the same territory as that occupied by previous charters and no evil has resulted from it that I know of. There is no danger of_ getting toe many lines constructed in this country. We need railway lines paralleling each other at a distance of twenty miles even in prairie country, and we need them worse than in mining sections in even closer contact. We need transportation in all parts of Canada. There is nothing that we need so much. I would approve of a law that would be very much more liberal with regard to the construction of railways than our present Act is. I approve of the law in the state of Minnesota because there any four or five gentlemen can organize themselves into a railway company and they can obtain a charter from; the Secretary of State and start to build the railway in three days. 1 had occasion to go there to get an extension of the Port Arthur, Duluth and Western Railway charter in the state of Minnesota and I found that we would have to organize a new company. I went to Minneapolis and left there in five days with the charter in my possession. This system has worked well in that state. The law protects private property. People obtaining charters only get the right to build a railway in a certain section of country. They cannot take the property of any company or individual and they cannot injure the property of any company or individual unless they pay for it. There is no grievance, but there is a free invitation to capitalists to build railways wherever they are wanted, wherever the railways would pay and wherever the people need the services of railways. In my judgment it would be a mistake to act upon the suggestion which some hon. gentlemen have made in this case. I want to tell hon. .gentlemen who are now advocating the imposition of conditions with regard to the building of this railway that they will find, if that principle is adopted, that they have given a monopoly that they little dreamed of to the big lines and to the big corporations who will build this road whenever they please and as they please. Hon. gentlemen in this House know-in fact I need not hesitate to state it -that a great many important lines that we have to-day in operation are not the work of great corporations or of great capitalists. They are the work of the local community who agitated for them, who organized them, who went before the public and who besieged parliament with deputations until they obtained their charters and the necessary aid, and until they got their enterprises into a position to attract capital and the larger operator into whose hands the roads finally passed. If it were not for that class of promotion we would

not have to-day many of the railways that are serving the people of the country and we would not have had them at such an early stage as we did. I say to the gentlemen who are advocating this restriction that they will be making a mistake in the interest of the community that they are seeking, honestly, I have no doubt, to help. Now, our Railway Act is not altogether without conditions. A company which obtains a charter must expend fifteen per cent of its capital within a limited time or it must give back the charter. The Act provides for forfeiture if it does not carry out its provisions, and that is all that w'ould happen in the case of the condition as to a specific number of miles, only it would, in my judgment, destroy the opportunity of securing capital for carrying on the enterprise.

maintopic: WINNIPEG AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I do not know if the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat had me in his mind, but he was looking over here and I therefore desire to say a word or two upon this question. I endorse a very great deal of what he said. He warned us in the west to be cautious about limiting these railway corporations. We have no desire to do that at all. If a man is running a corner grocery and an individual comes in and makes some statement in an effort to do business with him, as a business man he wants some evidence of the man's bona fides. My time is, I think, valuable to me, and I hope it is valuable to the people who have sent me here. I do not want to go up to the Railway Committee room and have gentlemen get up there and say:	We have two millions of dollars and we are going to commence work to-morrow. If the chairman of the Railway Committee or the Minister of Railways and Canals will get up and say that these gentlemen have satisfied me that they mean business and that they have the capacity to carry out the undertaking, then I will support it. I am desirous of advancing any scheme which will result in the building of railways in this country, but I do not want any gentlemen to come into the Railway Committee room with a set of plans saying that they are willing to run through the Rocky mountains where they can never build a railway. I have in mind two instances in which plans have been exhibited for railways that they could never attempt to build, and this fact is evidence to me that these men have not investigated the situation at all. I am not opposed to charters. I have talked long upon this matter in the Railway Committee and talked hard upon it. There is a principle involved. Are we going to give charters to everybody who wants them, and such is really the contention of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee). If so I will have to be satisfied, but I do not want to go back to my con-68
stituents and have to say that I have been voting blindly for railway charters through my own district without having made some effort to discover the standing of the men who promote these charters and their capacity to carry out the railways they undertake. One hon. gentleman has stated that this omnibus chartering_ of railways is misleading to the people in the west. There is no doubt about that. I have said so before, and I say again that the settlers are deceived by this chartering of railways which may never be constructed. Since this Bill came before the railway committee a gentleman in my district wrote me ask-in'* my advice about going into a certain section of country and in his letter he says:
The great drawback seems to be the great distance from a railway. I should like your opinion very much indeed as to railway building through this district. If one can believe all that the papers say and what the various plans show it would seem that it would soon be a network of railways and very little room left to grow grain.
This gentleman seems to have hit off the situation pretty accurately. We get some very valuable settlers into that country from the United States; they meet the land man who sends them out 30 or 40, or 50 miles from a railway; he shows them the plans of railways running through their location and the fact of the matter is that these people are simply humbugged. As their representative I object to that kind of thing. If those who ask for charters satisfy the Minister of Railways or some other competent authority of their ability and their intention to proceed with the construction of these railways, then they should have a charter and I shall do all that I can to help them along; but if a certain number of men apply to this parliament for a charter simply for the purpose of exploiting it then I am most determinedly opposed to any such proceedings.
Bill reported; read the third time and passed.

maintopic: LONDON AND LANCASHIRE PLATE GLASS COMPANY.

speechtext: House in committee on Bill (No. 27) to incorporate the London and Lancashire Plate Glass and Indemnity Company of Canada.-Mr. Macdonell.

maintopic: LONDON AND LANCASHIRE PLATE GLASS COMPANY.
speechtext:
As we all know there is a great English company known as the London and Lancashire Insurance Company and I notice that the incorporators^ of this Bill reside in the city of Toronto which would lead to the inference that the company we are now chartering is not a subsidiary company to the London and Lancashire of England. Was the question of the similarity of name discussed in the Banking and Commerce Committee? Of course,



the objects sought are different, but there very_ readily arises in the minds of people a misapprehension as to the character of the company, and it seems to me that those who are promoting this Bill should come with a different name from the one proposed. Of course, if that was discussed in committee and fully decided upon, it is not for me at this moment to raise any objection; but I simply ask that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LONDON AND LANCASHIRE PLATE GLASS COMPANY.
speechtext:
This question of the similarity of names very often comes before the Banking and Commerce Committee, and sometimes it is exceedingly difficult to decide on the proper view. However, there is no difficulty in the present case, because the incorporators are in Toronto, the company is practically a subsidiary company to the English company. It is promoted by that company, and the first gentleman named among the incorporators is the manager of that company in the province of Ontario. So I think we may safely assume that in this case at all events there will be no objection.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways).
speechtext:
In reply the board begs to state that an error has occurred in the memorandum submitted by the board marked 'A' and referred to in the above inquiry in citing the order as No. 192. The order in question is order No. 3,244, and is dated July 4, 1907. Order No. 192, dated October 18, 1904 was signed by the late Chief Commissioner, the Hon. A. G. Blair, but was not in fact issued. The order was not issued until subsequently, but in substance the two orders are identical. Referring, therefore, to the inquiry, the application was made to the board on October 4, 1904. Subsequently, on May 5, 1905, the application was heard at a public sitting of the board in Ottawa, Mr. White, K.c!)
Mr- J. E. McMullen appearing on behalf of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and Mr. U. Valiquet, engineer of the Mr. PUGSLEY.
Department of Public Works, appearing for the Department of Public Works. The board, after hearing what was alleged, as set forth in the notes of proceedings, volume 16, pages 1684 to 1696, reached the following decision, namely, that the applicants (that is, the Department of Public Works of Canada) be granted leave to cross, at rail level, with the proposed wharf the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's tracks, opposite the town of Pembroke, as shown on the plan filed, and that the crossing be protected by an automatic bell, the cost of the installation and maintenance to be borne by the applicants, that is, the Department of Public Works. It appears from the evidence that the contention of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was that the streets of the town of Pembroke did not extend beyond the water line of the Ottawa river; that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had constructed their line on a trestle in the water; that the wharf, having been constructed outside the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's trestle, the approach to it from the town side and the crossing of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's tracks was something the company should not be held liable for the cost of the protection of. It would appear that the issuance cf the order was delayed to enable the Department- of Public Works to decide whether they would take the order subject to the condition that they paid for the protection, or to endeavour to arrange with the town to pay for the cost of protection. Finally, however, at the request of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, under date of a letter of April 3, 1907, an order was issued.	.

He said : Mr. Speaker, I trust I take no exaggerated view of the subject involved

in this motion which I have the honour to present to the House when I state that I consider it of the very greatest importance not only to eastern Canada but to the whole Dominion. It is a question which has a direct bearing on that very great problem of affording the best means of transportation for the commerce of our country. I regret Sir, that I am unable to approach the subject with that ability and comprehensive knowledge which it undoubtedly demands. I feel that I cannot deal with this particular subject of the branch lines connecting with the Intercolonial Railway without in some way reviewing the transportation history of the past, and for convenience sake I shall divide that history into four periods. First of all, at the very dawn of confederation the problem which confronted the people of that day was the construction of the Intercolonial Railway to connect the eastern and western provinces which then constituted Canada, and allied with that was the question of the extension and completion of our canal system. It is not mere tradition to say that in the confederation compact the construction of the Intercolonial Railway was placed as a set off against the extension of the canal system. Rightly or wrongly it was viewed that the canal system of Canada appertained more directly to the transportation interests of what was known as Upper and Lower Canada and that the Intercolonial Railway was conceived as a means of solving the transportation problem for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, which were then the other two provinces in the confederation. The second period in our transportation history commenced with the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The third period was that in which the government of the day dealt with the transportation question by aiding the building of railways throughout Canada by the granting of money and land subsidies and co-related to that same period was the governmental guarantee of bonds (in addition to the subsidies granted) of railways that were deemed to be in the general interest of the country.
The fourth period may well be referred to as the period of the National Transcontinental Railway or Grand Trunk Pacific period. That great work was dealt with by the last parliament, with a view to meeting the larger transportation questions that have arisen by reason of the additions to our territory and the expansion and development of our commerce. I shall, as briefly as I can, deal with these four periods before I come to discuss the immediate question submitted to the House by my resolution.

I need not say that in the selection of a route for the railway there were great differences of opinion.
