Now, Mr. Speaker, I cannot very well take into consideration the declaration of this resolution without assuming one fact, which fact, if you take it from under this resolution, permits the resolution to be so absolutely futile and nugatory that its consideration even would be a waste of time by this House, and I would be but wasting your time and my own time and energy if I were to continue without the basis of that fact. I have declared in this resolution:
That in the opinion of this House it is desirable in furtherance of the transportation interests of this Dominion, that the sphere of influence of the Intercolonial Railway as a government operated railway should be widened and extended by securing, by lease or otherwise, such of the branch lines of railway now connecting with the Intercolonial Railway, as will serve as direct and profitable feeders to the traffic of said railway.
It must be taken as an assumed fact, and it is not and should not be a violent

assumption that the Intercolonial Railway is to continue as a government-owned and government-operated railway, that that is to be the policy of this parliament and of this government, as it has been the policy of past parliaments and past governments. I have the right to assume that. I need only refer to the political history of this country, the history of this parliament and the history of all governments, ' to lead me to the conclusion that it is a fair assumption that the Intercolonial Railway is to be continued as it was conceived-a government road, operated by the government and the people of Canada. If it is not to be, if the assumption is too violent, then, Sir, my remarks are of no avail, they have no point and they are without foundation either in fact or fiction. Let me, therefore, invite your attention to what has occurred since confederation. Take the history of the Conservative party, the attitude of all Conservative administrations down to 1896, and I am bound to say that on its face it was not an attitude of hostility, but an attitude of friendliness. If you turn to the debates of parliament in 1883, when Sir Charles Tupper was Minister of Railways, and refer to the votes and estimates of that period you will there recognize that in all of the works proposed, connected in any way with the Intercolonial Railway, whether it was the subsidizing of a branch line, whether it was the construction of terminals, whether it was the building of breakwaters or wharfs, the basis of the application to parliament for these money votes was the extension of the Intercolonial Railway and the improvement of its traffic that its earnings might be benefited. Sir Charles Tupper, in proposing to parliament line after line to be subsidized, said:	It is a
feeder to the Intercolonial Railway, part of the government system. Even that railway, known now as the Atlantic and Lake Superior, more generally known as the Baie des Chaleurs, when it was first brought to the notice of this House, was brought forward in the form of a resolution providing money for the construction of that railway by the government as a branch line of the Intercolonial Railway. Later the aid was changed to a subsidy to a railway company.
The branches thus constructed, the wharfs and breakwaters and harbours and terminals built and improved were all for the purpose of enabling the Intercolonial railway to continue its work. There were additions to the road; a short line was built from Oxford Junction to Stellarton, other lines were built in Cape Breton and Nova Scotia, the St. Charles branch from St. Charles to Levis was constructed and other extensions and improvements were made. It is true that about 1896 there were rumours that it was the intention of the Con
servative government of that day to transfer the Intercolonial Railway to a private corporation. I know not if these rumours were well or ill founded, but I do know that if there was any truth in them, the Liberal party of Canada gained advantage to the extent that these rumours were believed in. However, so far as the proceedings of this House will demonstrate the Conservative party was committed to the continuance of the Intercolonial as a government railroad. At all events, from the year 1896 when the Liberal government assumed power down to the present moment, every Act of that government was such as to impress the people of Canada with the idea that the Liberal party as a party is a friend of the Intercolonial and bent on' it? continuance as a government operated railway. Every act of the Liberal government: the construction of lines, the improvement of the Intercolonial itself, its extension into Montreal, the leasing for a long period of years of part of the Grand Trunk line and access to its Montreal terminals, the purchase of the Canada Eastern Railway; a thousand and one acts of the Liberal government demonstrate that it was in favour of maintaining the present status of the Intercolonial. Read over the acts of 1903 and 1904 in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway; read them over carefully and there is hardly a clause or a line which does not indicate that provision is made by the government and by the parliament of Canada for the future of the Intercolonial as a government road. The possibility of forfeiture, the possibility of failure on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific, are safeguarded in every direction by provisions that the government shall be in a position to nullify any disaster that may accrue by the absorption of the portion of the line that may be forfeited as a part of the Intercolonial railway system. There can be no question but that down to this period the attitude of the Liberal government, and the attitude of all parliaments in which I have sat indicate no other thought than that the Intercolonial should be continued as a railroad owned and operated by the government of Canada. I think therefore that I have the right to assume that there is no other intention on the part of the government or the parliament of Canada. I remember, when I had the honour to preside over the Department of Railways and Canals, there were similar rumours with respect to the Intercolonial Railway. There are always rumours set afloat for this purpose or for that and generally because of some ulterior purpose to be served. I remember that on one occasion a rumour was circulated (for what purpose I know not) that the Intercolonial Railway was to cease as a government operated road and to become the property of a private corporation. I remember,

speaking for the government-and I do not think I have ever exceeded my authority [DOT]-I remember making the statement that the government of Canada as then constituted had no intention of disposing of the Intercolonial Railway, that on the contrary that they were determined to maintain it in its entirety and in its present status as a portion of the transportation system of Canada, and that in so doing they were also determined that it should be made a paying asset.
Now, Sir, before discussing the direct question of the acquisition of the branch lines, I must ssume that this railway is to continue as a government railway to be operated by the government. If I were not able to assume that then there would be no point to my resolution and no object to be served by it. Taking that assumption as correct I would therefore bring to the notice of this House the question of the absorption of the branch lines connected within the Intercolonial Railway as a part of the Intercolonial Railway system. I shall bring it to the notice of the House purely as a business proposition; a proposition designed to be of advantage to the Intercolonial itself of advantage to the people served by the Intercolonial, of advantage to Canada, and incidentally of advantage to the communities served by these branch lines. Let me analyse the meaning of this resolution.. It does not involve the purchase of a single line of railway unless the parliament of Canada so authorizes. It does not declare that the government shall purchase all the branch lines, or even one of them. It does not involve any addition to the public debt. It simply declares that power should be taken by the government of Canada to extend the Intercolonial railway by acquiring by lease or otherwise such of the branch lines as would be deemed to be of advantage as feeders to the Intercolonial.
Now, we have the benefit of a declaration by the right hon. leader of this House with respect to this question. It will be borne in mind that I had the honour to move at the last session of the last parliament a resolution which covered the resolution which I am moving to-night, but which went further and involved the extension westward of the Intercolonial, with a view to facilitating the import and export trade of the Dominion through Canadian channels. There was some discussion in this House on that resolution and incidentally we had the benefit of a declaration by the Prime Minister on the question of the absorption of the branch lines. He stated that if the Intercolonial were owned and operated by a company, unquestionably it would be a part of its business to absorb the branch lines, and that any well-managed railway company would so do. He did raise the question as to whether govem-Mr. EMHERSON.
ment operation was elastic enough. That was simply raised as a doubt; but we had this declaration, that if the Intercolonial were to be run as a business proposition the branch lines would be so absorbed. Now, Sir, does the resolution propose any new thing in the history of railways either in this country or in any other country? We find that everywhere in Canada where the Grand Trunk Railway has been brought into contact with a branch line it has absorbed that line if it could. We find that throughout Canada, both in the east and in the west, wherever the Canadian Pacific Railway has had an opportunity of securing a branch line of railway, it has secured it. The history of all countries demonstrates the same thing. The railways in Great Britain were originally many. A few of the larger ones absorbed the smaller ones and the branches, and they became systems. In the United States we find great railway systems which have become so by means of absorption. The New York Central started out as a very puny railway, but by extending its influence and absorbing its branches it has become one of the great railway systems of the world. The same is true with respect to the Pennsylvania system. The Grand Trunk has absorbed the Buffalo and Lake Huron, the Midland with eight branches, the Great Western with five branches, the Northern, and Pacific Junction, the Hamilton and Northwestern, the Lake Erie and Georgian Bay, the Hamilton and Lake Erie, the Canada Atlantic and Parry Sound, and others. The number of branch lines absorbed by the Canadian Pacific is innumerable; I shall not attempt to recite them. If you go into the United States, you will find the same conditions prevailing there, in the Vanderbilt system, the Gould system, the Harriman system. It is true, in many instances these are con-

solidations of other railways, but they are as well the gathering in of the shorter branches, the more insignificant railways. In Great Britain the history of railways points to the same result. The Midland railway, originally a small railway in the neighbourhood of Derby and Nottingham, is now one of the great railways of the world. It absorbed several other railways, and numerous branches and feeders. I need not attempt to give the details. I simply point to the fact that in all countries the history has been that the trunk lines secure the feeders

for what purpose?
For the benefit of the trunk lines as well as of the feeders themselves. No argument is needed to convince any one that it is to the advantage of the people resident in the districts traversed by these branch lines that there shall be a consolidation, so that they will have to deal with but one system. It would be an advantage pecuniarily in respect of freight rates to the patrons of those railways, it would be an immense advantage in the assembling of the product and the traffic within the zone of influence of these trunk lines. In the province of New Brunswick, wherever the Canadian Pacific Railway was brought in contact with branch lines of railway, the Canadian Pacific Railway at once seized upon the branch lines to the advantage of these lines and, as I submit, to the greater advantage of the Canadian Pacific Railway itself. This is submitted to this House as a business proposition in the interests of the Intercolonial Railway, in the interests of the people of all Canada, in the interests of the people in the eastern sections of Canada, and particularly in the interests of the people served by these branch lines. I hold no brief on the part of any branch lines in Canada, I have no interest direct or indirect, near or remote in any branch line in Canada connected with the Intercolonial Railway, but I have an interest in the people of that section of Canada who are served by these branch lines. I recognize the disadvantage they are under, the discrimination against them with respect to freight rates. That authority was given for the continuation of a branch line from a point on the main line in Saskatchewan extending for a distance of 50 miles, but it is not unlikely that in the near future circumstances will make it desirable that this branch line should be continued 100 miles further.
That is the policy that has made for the success of the great railway corporations; whenever they see a prospect of traffic being developed they pre-empt the territory and depend upon the settlers coming in to create business for the road. I admit that while the Intercolonial Railway is operated by the government of Canada they cannot enter into all the different phases of the development of their system to be found in the operations of these great corporations but it would be a most unfortunate circumstance if the mere accident of the Intercolonial Railway being owned by the government of Canada should debar the people of the maritime provinces for all time from any hope or expectation of further railway advantages. I have in mind the conditions existing in eastern Nova Scotia, which illustrate the point I desire to make. When the Intercolonial Railway was built through the island of Cape Breton 26 years ago, it was built along the northern side of Bras d'Or lake, leaving the great expanse of fertile and mineral producing country in the southern part of that island without railway accommodation .Some seven or eight years ago a company was formed to build from Port Tupper on the Intercolonial Railway through the southern section of the island to tap the important mining areas lying in that section of the island. Unfortunately adverse circumstances arose, as they sometimes do with respect to the operations of private companies, and after that road was built for thirty miles from Port Tupper to the town of St. Peters, the company were for some reason unable to carry out their financial obligations and the road has not been extended further. They are operating a very excellent system of railway for that 31 miles, but as already intimated, the haul is so short that they are unable to get any through traffic, because every ton of freight they would get would be held up at Port Tupper for additional freight tolls and the consequence is that all that freight is carried by water transportation in competition with the ex-

isting road. But all the country east from St. Peters through the richest part of the island of Cape Breton along to Louisburg, and the large and important mining and industrial centres of Glace Bay, Bridgeport and Dominion No. 4, is at present without a vestige of railway accommodation, so far as the government of Canada is concerned. The only railway in that part of the country is a road owned by the Dominion Coal Compnay, built to carry coal from their mines to the winter port of Louisburg. That company will not undertake to perform the functions of a common carrier, and no other coal company operating there is permitted to have the products of its mine carried to Louisburg or Sydney; the consequence is that these mines, which are of immense value are still undeveloped and will continue undeveloped until the government of Canada adopt the policy enunciated by the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) and acquire the Cape Breton railway and extend it into these centres of population. Glace Bay has a population of 20,000, and it is almost incredible that that large town is to-day practically without any railway communication except the accommodation permitted to them by the coal company operating the coal mines. The same thing is true of all the other centres of population in the southern part of Cape Breton, and I am sure hon. gentlemen listening to me will not say that the prospect of building a railway through the southern part of Cape Breton into these mining centres offers no prospect of remuneration. Hon. gentlemen who are familiar with the conditions existing in that part of the country will admit that there is no part of eastern Canada that offers greater prospects of remuneration to a railway than these mining centres in southern Cape Breton, but not for fifty years can it be hoped that any new mines will be opened in southern Cape Breton for the reason that the Intercolonial Railway has pre-empted the most profitable part of the carrying trade at one end and the Dominion Coal Company at the other. It is not to be expected that another company would go in there to build a railway to operate in that limited territory. The solution of the difficulty, so far as that section of thd country is concerned, would be in the policy enunciated by the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson), the acquisition of the Cape Breton Railway and its extension into southern Cape Breton, giving easy access to the centres of Canada which would afford a ready market for the products of that particular district. I must apologize for giving my argument a sectional illustration but I think the illustration is so pointed and so well calculated to give effect to the argument I am endeavoring to make that I could not resist the temptation to use it.

There are other aspects of this question which have been dealt with by the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmer-son), and I do not desire to trespass further on the time of the House than to exhort the members of the government, so far as I am able, to take into their serious consideration the questions brought up by the hon. gentleman and enunciated in his resolution. As I said, I believe that if the future of the Intercolonial Railway is to continue as a road owned and operated by the government of Canada, it is only right and proper that the people of eastern Canada should expect that the government will perform their functions in respect to the operation of that road and the carrying on of the railway business as it is carried on by the other railway corporations of Canada. If, on the other hand, the government of Canada are content with existing conditions, I do fear that a very strong and intense movement will take place among the people of eastern Canada to hand over the Intercolonial Railway to a company that will afford them some prospect of better communication with the trunk systems operating in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I regard this discussion as the most important from the standpoint of the maritime provinces that has taken place during this session. It is of such importance to the constituency that I have the honour to represent and to the province from which I come that I feel I would not be doing my duty if I did not express my views in regard to it. I am in accord, in the main, with the resolution moved by the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Em-merson) and his remarks in support of it. I would not indiscriminately take over all the branch lines that exist along the Intercolonial Railway. I would select such branches as show apparent prospects of paying the expenses of operation. No doubt that there are some branches along the Intercolonial Railway that would not pay running expenses. I can well understand that a branch railway, weighted down with a head office staff and all the other adjuncts of a railway, might not pay expenses and might be a losing venture, whereas, when it is run as a part of a great system like the Intercolonial Railway, it might be a profitable railway. But I would go further than my hon. friend has gone in his resolution and I would amend it by providing that we should not only take over such branch lines as already exist along the line of the Intercolonial Railway but that we should build branch lines where they do not now exist. In fact, Sir, it appears to me that this is our first duty in regard, to the question that comes before us in this resolution. The people who live along these branches that are now being operated
by a company have some kind of accommodation, they have a railway service. But
I	had in mind certain parts of the province of Nova Scotia that had not these disadvantages at all. I submit, Sir, that it will be the first duty of the government, not to take over the branh lines and weigh the Intercolonial down with them, but to provide for those sections of the maritime provinces that have not yet been given the advantages of railway communication.
A great many proposals have been made during the last few months in the newspapers as to what should be done with the Intercolonial Railway. My hon. friend from Westmoreland referred to the reso lution passed by the various boards of trade throughout the country. One of the proposals made by the board of trade of Halifax was that the Intercolonial between Moncton and Halifax should be doubletracked, to provide for the increased traffic that will seek an outlet in that direction on the completion of the Grand Trunk Pacific. It was found, however, that there wrere objections to the proposal to doubletrack the main line of the Intercolonial, partly, chiefly, on account of the fact that the grades on the Intercolonial are very heavy. Another proposal was made that the road should be diverted around by Parrsboro in an endeavour to find grades suitable as a continuation of the Grand Trunk Pacific. We have not yet the report of the surveys made by way of Parrsboro, but it is reported that engineering difficulties were found in that direction. No doubt the grades on the Intercolonial are very heavy at certain places. Any person familiar with the topography of Nova Scotia, will know that the Intercolonial crosses a mountain range known as the Cobequid mountains. This mountain range extends across the counties of Cumberland and Colchester. Amherst is almost at sea level, and so is Truro, but, in order to get across the range of mountains from Amherst even the best engineering skill available when the Intercolonial was built was compelled to rise 618 feet to the summit before the descent to Truro could be begun. This rise involves grades, in some cases, I understand,
II	per cent. It would not be a business proposal to spend the enormous sums we are spending in building the line from the Pacific ocean to Moncton with grades of four tenths of one per cent, and then continue that railway along a road with grades of 1-5 per cent. I have a proposal to make to the Minister of Railways, and through him to the government, by which this road could reach the Atlantic sea-board with grades similar to those by which it crosses the rest of Canada. Besides the grades of the Cobequid mountains, there is another heavy grade near Dorchester, New Brunswick. My proposal is to divert the Intercolonial at some
HAGGART I never said that or anything pointing in that direction. What I was referring at the time was the charging of expenditure to capital instead of to income.

If I have misrepresented my hon. friend, I have been led astray by the language he himself used. Here is what he said:
What do the people of this country care about investing their money in capital expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway?
W hat they want to know is how the money which is taken out of their pockets is expended. They believe that capital expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway should cease. Yet there has been a drain on the resources of the country on that account of over $3,000,000 a year since these hon. gentlemen went into power. What possible asset to the people has been the expenditure on capital account on the Intercolonial Railway for the last ten years? When I was managing the Intercolonial Railway in 1896 and the years preceding, I insisted that the expenditure on capital account should cease, as a capital expenditure, and that it should be charged to the revenue of that road.
Now whaft does that language mean? The hon. gentleman asks ' what do the people care about investing their money in capital expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway.' Evidently, if these words mean anything, they mean that in investing their money in capital expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway, the people were making a bad bargain and throwing away their money.
Not at all. Surely the hon. gentleman knows better.

My hon. friend asks ' what do the people care about investing their money in the Intercolonial?' Does that mean that they are in favour of it?

<*.. -

What I meant was that it made no difference to the people whether the expenditure was charged to capitial or to income. The mjoney was spent on the road and what I was contending was that it ought properly to be charged to income and the capital account closed. I never made any such absurd statement as that no money should be spent on the Intercolonial Railway, nor is there anything in the context which will give that meaning.
I am taking the hon. gentleman's own words.
You can read them over half a dozen times, but perhaps you do not understand them.
The hon. gentleman says that the people of Canada believe the capital expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway should cease.

So it should, and that is what the late Alexander Mackenzie himself said in this House. He said that the capital account ought to be closed on the Intercolonial Railway and that the expenditure on that account should he charged to income. But to conclude from that, that I argued, or that Mr. Mackenzie argued, there should be no more capital expenditure on the road is absurd.
I would like my hon. friend to tell me how he is going to charge the capital expenditure to income when there is no income?
He will then show the actual deficit. That is all.

When this policy of my hon. friend was announced, we from the maritime provinces knew very well it would be very unpopular among our people. We must have additional capital expenditure on the Intercolonial from time to time. I have no sympathy either with the statement we so often hear that the Intercolonial Railway is a burden to this country, that we have to meet parliament every year with a deficit, and certain of our hon. friends make a great deal of political capital out of the small deficit which exists from year to year on the Intercolonial Railway.
A small deficit? $1,750,000 in one year.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) forgets that in other years there were surpluses. It was never intended that the Intercolonial Railway should pay dividends. When it was built it was well known by the people of Quebec and Ontario that it would be a losing speculation from a monetary point of view. In the discussions in parliament and in the press of that day it was stated over and over again that these provinces went into this venture with their eyes open, knowing there would be a loss of money from year to year, but expecting other advantages to counter-balance that loss, which advantages they have since realised. As my hon. friend from Westmoreland has said, the Intercolonial Railway was built as a part of compact of confederation, and if the House will permit me, I will read the clause in the British North America Act which authorizes the building of the Intercolonial Railway:
Inasmuch as the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have joined in a declaration that the construction of the Intercolonial Railway is essential to the consolidation of the union of British North America and to the assent thereto of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and have consequently agreed that provision should be made for its immediate construction by the government of Canada: therefore, in order to give effect to that agreement, it shall be the duty of the government and parliament of Canada to provide for the commencement, within six months after the union, of a railway connecting the river St. Lawrence with the city of Halifax in Nova Scotia, and for the construction thereof without intermission, and the completion thereof with all practicable speed.
There is nothing there about dividends. And there is nothing in the discussions which took place at the time to show that the opinion was then entertained that the Intercolonial Railway would be a paying venture. On the contrary, they show just the opposite. Permit me also to read an extract from the Toronto ' Globe ' of that date to show what that great organ of public opinion then thought of the Intercolonial Railway. The date of this editorial is the 26th of September, 1865, after the date when the conference was held but prior to the date when confederation was consummated:
The scheme of the government for the construction of the Intercolonial Railway opens an account that never will be closed. Every storm of snow in the inhospitable regions below Riviere du Loup will lay a new burden on the people of Upper Canada. The tax payers will watch the passenger travel and freight traffic with the liveliest interest as indicating the extent of	the demands
upon them for the year. It is a dream of many persons in Nova Scotia that this Halifax	and	Quebec Railway will draw to itheir harbour the trade of the west, but it is a dream and nothing more. No passenger, no shipper of freight will ever think of going to Halifax when he can find shipping at Quebec or Portland.
With Upper Canada decidedly opposed to the scheme, and Lower Canada divided, we are happv to say that we do not see any great danger of hasty action. We are only astonished that the ministry should have committed themselves to a scheme which finds

bo little support in any part of the province, the lower province delegates humbugged them beautifully. It is evident that the Kiuenose is a sharp fellow. He is rubbed bright on his rocks. We shall have to be careful in our dealings with him. If Lower Canada is afraid of him because he is British, we must learn to watch him because he is not very rich, but is very keen and shrewd. -Toronto ' Globe/ Sept. 26, 1865.
That was the opinion /of the Toronto ' Globe ' of that day.
Does the hon. gentleman agree with that?

The ' Globe ' itself will
not make that statement to-day. As a matter of fact, every one knows that the poor blue nose was victimized in the bargain. This was acknowledged later by the fact that the maritime provinces were given afterwards much better terms than they were accorded in the original bargain of 1867. In.looking over the debates in parliament at the same time I find that the opinion prevailed that the Intercolonial Rail-wav would not be a paying venture. The Hon. Geo. Brown, in the legislature of Canada, in 1865, made the following statement:
As a commercial enterprise the Intercolonial has not, I apprehend, any considerable merit. As a work of defence it has however many advocates, but if the union of the provinces is to go on, it is an absolute necessity and as the price of the union, were there no other arguments in its favour, I heartily go for it.
That was the opinion of the Hon. Geo. Brown prior to the time the road was built. Allow me also to give you an expression of opinion from the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie in his speech on supply in parliament in 1870, when the question of the construction of the Intercolonial was up. Mr. Mackenzie said:	,
Everybody knows that the Intercolonial Railway would be utterly valueless in a commercial point of view, it was to be built because they had bargained to build it and they should keep to their bargain.
I also find in a speech by the late Walter Shanly, M.P., in 1870, in this House, a gentleman who was, at that time, I believe, the member for Grenville, that the following language was used:
The railway project by itself was not popular in Upper Canada. But when the greater question assumed shape and form after the conference at Quebec, and when it became apparent that in order to bring about the Confederation of the British North American provinces each of the parties to the compact would be called upon to make some sacrifice of local prejudice or local interest, then Upper Canada accepted of the Railway part of the project as a political and social necessity. A leading politician of Upper Canada, generally recognized as an exponent of the public opinion of the day and said * Rather than not have

confederation he would agree to build ten Intercolonial Railways/ That very fairly expressed the sentiment of Upper Canada.
At confederation there were two courses open to the people of the maritime provinces. Prior to that time the trade of the maritime provinces was with the United States. The provinces were prosperous. They had had the advantages of reciprocal trade with the United States, and they were enjoying a large degree of prosperity. They had their choice of continuing their trade with the United States, having little or no trade with the upper provinces, or building the Intercolonial and changing the course of their trade altogether. They embarked upon this project of building the Intercolonial. Everybody knows that the flour that fed the 800,000 people who were then living in the maritime provinces came from Boston, or some other port in the United States, that it was ground at American mills, from wheat that was probably raised on the western prairies of the United States, and that they received very little from the upper provinces at that time. The agricultural implements used on the farms of the maritime provinces were made in the factories of the United States. Yankee mowing machines, rakes, pitchforks, axes and buckets were to be found on every farm in the maritime provinces, and the question was whether we were going to continue that condition of affairs or try to find means of carrying on a trade with the other provinces of Canada. We embarked on the construction of the Intercolonial with these ideas. We knew very well that it would cost us money. The people of the upper provinces were quite well aware that it would be a long time before it would be a prosperous venture and I submit that the price is not a heavy price that we have paid. There have been deficits in connection with the Intercolonial Railway, but they have not been large deficits. Some of my hon. friends on the other side of the House look surprised at that statement, but if they will add up all the deficits that have occurred on the Intercolonial Railway since it was constructed about thirty-one years ago, and strike an average, they will find that the average annual deficit was $245,434-not a very large sum of money each year when we consider what we have received from this great national asset. Take the population of Canada at six and a-half millions, it is the price of two postage stamps for every man, woman and child in the Dominion of Canada. Four cents apiece each year will give us more than the amount of the average annual deficit on the Intercolonial Railway.
What would be Dm amount, adding in the capital expenditure?

I do not regard the capital expenditure as a deficit, I have not made that a calculation. Of course, that would be much larger, but my hon. friend must remember, which he always seems to forget, that while we have spent $80,000,000 in the construction of the Intercolonial Railway we have a slendid investment for our money. When this road was built there were certain things expected of it. It was not expected that it would make money, but there were' certain other things that were more valuable than money that were expected to result from the construction of the Intercolonial Railway. It was expected that it would bind the provinces of Canada more closely together, that it would unite the provinces into one great Dominion. It was also expected that the maritime provinces would become a profitable market for the manufactures of Ontario and Quebec. It was expected that the New England manufacturer would be driven from the field and that he would be replaced by the manufacturer of Ontario and Quebec. We also thought in the maritime provinces at that time that we might be able to sell our goods, our coal, our iron and our fish to the people of the upper provinces. That was looked forward to by the people of the maritime provinces. We expected that the ports of the maritime provinces would be used, instead of the ports of the United States, in the shipment of goods from the western provinces. All these things have come about to a certain extent. These provinces have been united together, they have been cemented as we expected they would be, and I suppose there is not a man within the hearing of my voice that would not stand up for a united Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific and you could not have had a united Canada without the construction of the Intercolonial. Is not that worth the price of two postage stamps each year to the people of Canada? I think everybody will agree that the deficit is a mere bagatelle compared with the great results that have come from the construction of the road.
How much did the deficit on the canals amount to ?

I am not talking about the canals now. I am talking about the Intercolonial Railway on its merits. The provinces have been united and the maritime provinces have become a profitable market for the goods of the western provinces. In this connection, I had the honour, a few days ago, to move in the House for a return showing the amount of trade we had east bound and the amount of trade west bound on the Intercolonial and I got certain figures. I was not able to get them as complete as I would like to have had them,
but I find that in the year 1902, 54-03 of the traffic on the Intercolonial was east bound; in 1903, 51 -36 per cent of the traffic was east bound; in 1904, 48-83 per -cent; in 1905, 51-20 iper cent; in 1906, 44-32 per cent; in 1907, 44-44 per cent; in 1908, 44-55 per cent. A small increase has taken place within the last few years in west bound traffic, I think, owing to the shipment of large quantities of steel from Cape Breton to the west.
Does my hon. friend mean through traffic by west bound and east bound ?

I mean the total traffic going east and the total traffic going west. It will be found on pursuing this inquiry further that the Intercolonial has done even more for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec than it has done for the maritime provinces. It has done more to develop the trade of the western provinces than it has done for the east.
Unless you can quote the through traffic, that does not prove that a single ton went to Ontario.

My argument is that goods come from Ontario to the maritime provinces in very much greater quantity than we have been able to send goods to Ontario, and hence I contend that the representatives of Ontario ought to have a more friendly feeling towards the Intercolonial Railway if they truly represented the interests of their province. The New England manufacturer has been driven from the maritime provinces; all the implements, all the machinery used on the farms of the maritime provinces to-day are of Canadian manufacture and the Yankee product has disappeared. I repeat that all the goods we use in the maritime provinces of nearly every class are manufactured in Canada, and largely in Ontario and Quebec. We are somewhat disappointed in the maritime provinces that our trade with the west has not expanded in a greater degree; we are disappointed somewhat that the markets of Ontario and Quebec have not taken as much of our fish, of our coal, and of our iron as we had hoped, but nevertheless a good trade is being worked up. On the whole, all that it was expected the Intercolonial would achieve for the people of Canada has come about, and I believe we have made a good investment even though we have to pay four cents a head every year to meet the bagatelle of a deficit which accrues. Now, why is it that the Intercolonial Railway during the thirty years of its existence has not developed more traffic and made more money. There must be some good reason for it, and were I to be frank I would express the opinion that the Intercolonial Railway has not been run with that energy and enterprise which ought to have marked its management. Of course,

this remark applies with more force to the government that existed prior to 1896 than it does to the present administration. The present administration has done much to build up the Intercolonial; they have extended it into Montreal and brought it into the heart of the commercial capital of Canada so as to enable it to get a share of the traffic which comes through that great city. They have improved the Intercolonial, they have given it heavier rails, modern rolling stock, and better trains and in other ways have enabled it to become the great national asset it is. But, at the same time I fear that that energy which characterises the management of the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific Railway is not to be found in the management of the Intercolonial. That of course may be an incident of government ownership but whatever the reason it seems to be the case. For example, the Intercolonial touches the sea at only a few points: at St. John, at Halifax, at Mulgrave, and at the Sydneys.
And Shediac and Chatham.
I might mention some other places.
A good many.

The illustrations I have taken will suffice for my argument. The population of that part of the maritime provinces is chiefly found along the coast and a vigorous administration of the Intercolonial would have had steamers plying on the adjacent waters and collecting traffic at these ports. I have in my mind the town of Mulgrave, in my own constituency, where for many years there was no attempt made to collect traffic from the adjacent shores east and west of the point where the railway strikes the sea and where the people are located. After a while private enterprise assisted by small subsidies from the government placed boats on these waters and as a result a splendid business for the Intercolonial Railway has grown up. But, the point I make is that the_ Intercolonial management itself did not think of putting the steamers there and collecting the traffic. I am told that when the Reid Railway was built in Newfoundland the Reid Company put on quite a number of steamers to connect with the railway and to deliver to it the traffic from the fishing villages along the coast, without which the railway could not have been made a financial success. No attempt .of that kind was made by the management of the Intercolonial to concentrate traffic at these points where the railway touches the sea. This is only one illustration among others that might be given to show that the road has not been managed with that same business ability which Mr. SINCLAIR.
might be applied to it and which would probably be applied to it were it conducted as a private venture. Let me point out as an illustration of what I mean, that last year the small boats which run into Mulgrave called ' The Cann ' boats carried 7,898 passengers, most of whom took the Intercolonial Railway to points of destination, and 5,708 tons of freight which constituted a very profitable business for the railway that it otherwise would not get. Then again, there has not been the energy displayed that should have been displayed in the building of branch lines. Like my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) I can point to a special instance to prove my case. I have in mind a territory between the city of Halifax and the Strait of Canso, comprising about 150 miles in my own constituency, and possessing great resources in lumber, and mines, and fish, and agriculture, and although the Intercolonial has skirted the northern side of that territory for 30 years, not even an engineer has been sent into that district to survey it, nor has an agent of the Intercolonial gone there to discover its resources. Were the Intercolonial owned by a great private corporation I feel certain that long ere this something would have been done to give railway accommodation to the 40,000 people who inhabit that territory. As did my. hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte)'i ask:	Is this to go on for ever?
That country has been inhabited for over 100 years; the people living there have contributed their full share of the $400,000,000 that we have paid out for transportation facilities of various kinds in this country, but they have been shut off from participation in any share of that expenditure. In view of these facts the House will not be surprised when I urge that the government should not only consider the question of securing the railways already built but that they should deal first with the question of constructing railways in those parts of the maritime provinces which have never had railway communication. I think myself that this question is more important even than the securing of the branch lines, because while the people living on the branch lines have some kind of railroad servicp, the people I speak of are absolutely without any. We have been paying out millions of dollars for building canals; we have been spending millions more in deepening the St, Lawrence; we are now investing millions in building another great railway across the continent, and what I am advocating tonight is but a part of the great transportation system of Canada which has been made a part of the policy of this government, as it has of previous governments. Let us not deal with this question in any narrow spirit; let us not hesitate to embark on any

expenditure that may be necessary to perfect the Intercolonial system by building tributary lines which will develop the country through which they pass and by acquiring such branch lines as may prove to be feeders to the traffic of that system. If we do this, we will be developing the Intercolonial and making it what it is destined to be, a great national asset; we will be carrying out the policy that the people of this country endorsed with so much enthusiasm on the 26th of October last: the policy of keeping Canadian trade in Canadian channels and providing transportation facilities by which that trade can find an outlet to the sea by way of Canadian ports.

It is getting late, it is nearly midnight, but I have hopes that the House will listen to a word or two from me all the more readily because I speak rarely, and that I do not speak at all unless I think I have something to say. This question oi taking over branch lines is a very important question in the constituency which I represent. It is a question that is affecting almost every man in the county of Hants. I may say that it is a very important question all through western Nova Scotia. I do not propose to attempt to make a speech upon this question. I rose more for the purpose of making an appendix to this report which has been handed to me to-day, although I have no mandate from the Minister of Railways to make an appendix. I may say that I agree with a great deal that has been said by the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmer-son). I endorse his policy of taking over all these branch lines. I would endorse what he probably would not endorse-the policy of giving running powers over the Intercolonial from Moncton to Halifax to the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian Northern Railway, and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and any other railway that will bring traffic into Nova Scotia. .Before the dissolution of parliament last year, I understood that the government were in sympathy with the proposal toi take over the branch lines of the Intercolonial, and a commission was appointed to examine those lines and to report upon them. I found, after the report had been made, that the commission had not examined the Dominion Atlantic Railway. I may say that I live in the ancient town of Windsor on that line of railway, I found that the commission had not reported on it, although they had been ordered to do so, I learned that when they went to the manager of the railway and he demanded a sum of money-I do not think it was an unreasonable sum-for transporting them over his railway, a dispute arose, and the commission declined to examine his road at all.
I was afterwards told, although I do not think it was said in earnest, that the Dominion Atlantic Railway was not a branch of the Intercolonial. Now, if a branch means a shorter road going into a larger one, the Dominion Atlantic is not only a branch in the true sense, but it is more than an ordinary branch, because it empties its traffic into the Intercolonial by two mouths-first, by what is known as the Windsor branch of the Intercolonial, which is leased, I may say under the most unbusinesslike contract that) any government ever gave to a private company. I am glad to say that it was not the work of this government, but the work of the Conservative government, and I only hope that this government in 1914 will cancel that lease as promptly as it matures.
I was saying that the Dominion Atlantic empties its traffic into the Intercolonial by two mouths: the Windsor branch extending from Windsor to Windsor Junction, and the Midland Branch extending from Windsor to Truro. Would it be of advantage to the Intercolonial to purchase this road? I will reply in the language of the report of the engineer of maintenance, who says: ' The more branch lines the Intercolonial can gather, the better it will be for the Intercolonial; the more grist it will bring to their mill '-that is the expression. I know of no branch line from Montreal to Halifax that will bring more grist to the mill of the Intercolonial than the Dominion Atlantic. It runs through one of the most magnificent countries in Canada, and one of the richest agricultural districts, populated by an intelligent people, and the road, even managed as it is, is doing a most thriving business. This road I may say, is owned by a private company, a foreign company. I hope nobody will misunderstand me: when I say foreign I mean out of Canada. It is owned by a company in London who care nothing for Nova Scotia or the country it runs through except to get all the money possible out of everybody who uses the railway. That is patent to every one who knows the management of the railway, and I have known it ever since it was built. This road is 298 miles long by all its tracks. It runs from the town of Yarmouth in the west end of Nova Scotia to Halifax. It originally ran from the town of Annapolis to the town of Windsor. It afterwards became possessed of a branch line running from Windsor to the Intercolonial, a distance of forty-six miles. It also became possessed of the Western Counties Railway running from Digby to Yarmouth, and also of what was called the missing link between Digby and Annapolis, twenty miles in length, built I believe wholly by the government of Canada. The capital invested in the Dominion Atlantic Railway is nearly $8,000,000. According to the report of 1907, its passenger

earnings for that year were $341,981. Its passenger and miscellaneous earnings amounted to $380,157; its freight earnings amounted to $398,413. Its total earnings were $778,571, and its total operating expenses $569,985, showing net earnings of $208,586. It carried 334,805 passengers and 362,497 tons of freight. This is a railway already doing a most profitable business, and it would be one of the most important feeders of the Intercolonial. It would be of great advantage to the Intercolonial to have that road, and it would be of very great advantage to the people of the country through which the road runs. It might be assumed that at the present time all the traffic over that road goes to the Intercolonial, but that is not the case. No traffic, either freight or passenger, that it can divert from the Intercolonial is given to it. The timetables are so arranged that passengers can be accommodated off the Dominion Atlantic Railway on the Canadian Pacific Railway, and so that it is very inconvenient for them to get from the Dominion Atlantic to the Intercolonial Railway. Trouble arises between the two roads over the freight; there is friction between them constantly, the Dominion Atlantic working all the time in the interests of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The great disadvantages under which the people in the counties of Yarmouth, Digby, Kings, Annapolis and Hants are resting in connection with this road are that they are obliged to pay two freights or two express charges on everything that goes out of Nova Scotia to New Brunswick or to Ontario. Our merchants and manufacturers are handicapped and discouraged. We have all the advantages there necessary for a manufacturing country. We have magnificent water-powers along the line of that railway, we have coal near at hand, we have everything that would go to establish and to make profitable manufacturers if we were not handicapped and discouraged as we are by this privately owned railway. As it is we are operating along that road, cotton mills, duck mills, foundries, and furniture factories, and we are sending our manufactures up through Ontario into the prairie provinces; we have sent our cotton clear out to China. But the manufacturers are discouraged and are not prospering as they should. Our agriculturists are not prospering as they should. Every farmer and every fruit grower is handicapped and as I said before we have one of the best agricultural counties in Canada.
I may surprise some people who think we are a people exclusively engaged in fishing off the rocks when I say that along the line of the Dominion Atlantic Railway we have river bottoms that have raised their annual crop of hay without one pound of fertilizer for over 200 years since the early days when the French threw up their Mr. BLACK.
dykes and reclaimed those river bottoms from the encroaching tide. We have everything there requisite to make a prosperous and happy country if we were not so badly handicapped in matters of transportation. Our factories would grow, our agricultural products would increase if there were not such a discouragement every day to the farmer and to the manufacturer, by that privately owned railway. We exported last year over that railway to London and Liverpool $1,000,000 worth of apples alone, and there are new orchards growing there that in ten years will be sending $2,000,000 or $3,000,000 worth of apples to the foreign markets. All I ask of the government, all I ask of the Minister of Railways, is that the Dominion Atlantic Railway shall be placed in the same category as the other branch lines. It ought to be treated with superior consideration, but I shall only ask that it shall have the same examination and consideration and receive as much support as its length, as its business and as the people of the country traversed by it deserve.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. H. McALISTER (Kings and Albert).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it would be good judgment for me at this late hour to attempt to say many words on this subject. It would be unfortunate for the other members of the House, physically and mentally, if this debate should be continued longer to-night; but I feel it my duty, I do not think I could go home and sleep well if I did not rise in my place even if I should say nothing more than 'Amen.' I feel that I particularly am justified in speaking to-night as I have in my constituency four branch lines. There is probably not another member who can say that. I declare from the bottom of my heart and not in any partisan spirit that I believe it would be a benefit to the Intercolonial Railway if it should take over the branch lines in Kings and Albert. I know that the branch line from Salisbury to Harvey runs through one of the most progressive agricultural district in New Brunswick, and if taken over by the Intercolonial Railway would be a paying proposition and would not bring a yearly deficit to the Intercolonial Railway. Another branch, the Elgin & Havelock, would certainly not produce a deficit. We have another branch called the St. Martin's and Hampton branch, which terminates in one of the most elegant summer resorts, the village of St. Martins. I would not be so sure about the old Central or the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company. I am ready and willing to do all in my power to secure the adoption of the principle of this resolution. I am satisfied that if this resolution had not been talked of in my constituency and if my constituents did not feel that I would support it enthusiastically, they would not

have returned me to this House. I am safe in saying that it was the means of my securing the majority which I did in Albert county.

Mr. Speaker, I would not undertake at this late hour to follow the notes I intended to use this evening, but I believe I would be recreant to my duty if I did not rise before the conclusion of the debate to express my sentiment of admiration for the really excellent speech delivered this evening by the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson). He has spoken with eloquence of facts relating to the history of the Intercolonial Railway since its inception before confederation. He has shown by facts and figures which he has laid before the House that he was speaking on a subject on which he was well informed and the information he has given to the House and to the people through this House, will be of great value. I have admired especially the broad Canadian tone of his speech; he dealt with this great question of the Intercolonial Railway from the broad standpoint of Canadian interests. He reminded me of the speech delivered in this House last session by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), when he said he would deal with the Intercolonial Railway not from a sectional standpoint, not from the point of view of the maritime provinces, but from the point of view of Canada at large; and I am sure that the words of the Minister of Railways and Canals, coming as he does from the province of Ontario, have contributed largely to create or at least to strengthen the more favourable current of opinion which seems to permeate the public mind of that province.
It has been to the disadvantage of the Intercolonial, no doubt, that, owing to circumstances beyond the control of ministers or governments, the country could not expect great financial returns from the operations of the Intercolonial up to this time. As has been established by my predecessors in this debate, the fathers of confederation, and the great engineers who located the Intercolonial, saw that the advantage of this railway was, not in its possibilities of commercial returns, but in the fact that it would join together the eastern and the western provinces and would assist in building up Canada as a great nation. And to-day we find a realization of what Joseph Howe said years ago, that the great Atlantic ports of the maritime provinces were not there for the benefit of these provinces alone but to assist in the future greatness of all the British possessions in North America We have the testimony of Sir Sandford Fleming, the great British engineer. who himself located the Intercolonial, recommending the line which was afterwards adopted by the parliament of Canada, that for many years we could not expect 70
the Intercolonial to earn even its operating expenses, that the population of the eastern Drovinces was not dense enough to command financial returns, that it is not to be regarded from the commercial point of view but from the patriotic point of view, in its effect in building up the nation of which we are so proud and which we expect to see one of the greatest nations in the world before the end of the twentieth century. Though for years deficits have been accumulating, we should not lose sight of the national advantage of the railway and its important effect in the development of the country. Had the people and parliament of Canada early taken the stand taken by my hon. friend from Westmoreland to-night in this House, no doubt the deficits on the 1 Intercolonial would have been a thing of the past, surpluses would be the rule and the road would extend into many parts of the country which now it does not serve. But the parliament of Canada has not always taken a fair view of these deficits.
Now, undoubtedly, the time has come when the financial aspect of the Intercolonial is about to change. The railway magnates who are looking into the matter see that in the Intercolonial there is an estate which will undoubtedly bring in good financial returns in a very short time. I do not think that the deficits are due to any failure of administration on the part of the government-and in saying that I refer to former governments as well as to the present. These deficits necessarily followed from the condition of things. But better conditions will come with the time of greater expansion. Conditions have changed. The maritime provinces are part of a great *nation. They are on the threshold of an agricultural, commercial and industrial revival which will bring them to the prominent position which they are destined to occupy in this Dominion. The maritime provinces have now reached the threshold of an agricultural revival which will keep on the soil every child born under their blest heavens. Greater production will mean moTe wealth for the average individual, and greater comfort on the part of the people will mean more general travel and greater activity of commerce in every direction. Within five or six years, you will have the Intercolonial in a paying position, like any other great railway, whether managed by a government or by a corporation. We hear talk of a commission What does a commission mean? It is the combined wisdom of four or five men. I wonder why the Minister of Railways and Canals, the Deputy Minister of Railways, and three other men cannot form as good a body of management as any other that could be created. I have faith in the future of the Intercolonial and I sav it will be suicide for any government, whether Liberal or Conserva-



tive, to allow the people of Canada to think that they would entertain the idea of giving over to a private corporation this Intercolonial Railway for which we have sacrificed so much and which has made such good returns to the people of Canada.
I said that the maritime provinces are experiencing a new movement in commerce, industry and agriculture. Had we followed, in the first year of confederation, the advice of that great engineer, Sir Sanford Fleming, and developed at once the great advantages of the localities through which the Intercolonial Railway was built, we might from the very first have avoided these deficits which have confronted us # from year to year. Every foot of our land contains resources bound to be developed at some time or other. Those resources, which for years have been appealing to human intelligence and activity, are at last being developed, and we are finding out that every section of country through which the Intercolonial passes is one which will amply repay its exploitation. I do not wish to detain the House by reading quotations, especially as a couple of years ago I had occasion to express my views on this very question and urged on the government the taking over of those branches, which were not in the hands of people owning sufficient capital to operate them in a profitable manner and as they could be operated as parts of the trunk line. Had we listened to the advice given by Sir Sanford Fleming and established a fast mail and passenger service from the coast of Ireland to St. John's, Newfoundland, and thence to the north shore of New Brunswick over the Intercolonial Railway, where the seaports are open until the 15th of January, I have no doubt that we would have been spared all these deficits which have been accumulating from year kyyear. But I am not without hope that this great engineer, although now very old, will still live long enough to see the realization of his projects of "forty years ago.
It has been said that a bad choice was made in selecting the route of the Intercolonial Railway. No doubt had it not been for the unfortunate Ashburton Treaty which deprived us of a portion of our territory, another route would have been chosen. However, that was out of the question. In selecting the north shore the fathers of confederation wanted to favour the development of the Matapedia valley and the Gaspesia district. Had the government in 1882 or 1883, instead of paying a large subsidy to a company to build a railway from Matapedia station to Gaspg basin, built the railway themselves, they would have saved the people of that district all the trouble and losses they have had to suffer at the hands of a company unable to meet its engagements, and to-day Mr. TURGEON.
that district would be in a flourishing condition.	*
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the Postmaster General that if, instead of giving bonuses to the railway from Matapedia to Gaspe Basin, the government had built the road themselves the people of that district, represented by the Postmaster General, would have been spared all the misfortunes which they have had to suffer owing to the inability of the companies to meet their engagements. The same condition applies to the north shore of New Brunswick. Notwithstanding all the mistakes of the past I claim that to-day the best policy is one of expansion and progress. Such a policy has been extended by the government to the whole country .except in so far as the Intercolonial Railway is concerned, and I hope that the government will adopt that policy and display the same activity and energy with respect to the districts traversed by the Intercolonial Railway and give them the service they require. Such a policy would stimulate the creation of industries large and small and create a trade for the Intercolonial Railway which will place it in a magnificent nosition, commercially, financially and patriotically. We have, on this portion of the north shore of New Brunswick, unknown perhaps to many of the Canadian people, certainly unknown to the people of the west, not sufficiently known yet by a great many hon. members coming from the province of Ontario and even by some of my good neighbours from the province of Quebec, resources of the most valuable character, the development of which will, in a few years, compare favourably with that which has taken place in any portion of this country. In addition to the activity of the people in that region resulting in bringing from the bottom of the sea millions of dollars worth of fish products we have immense resources in iron ore, the very best, I will not say in Canada, but on the continent of America. We have at Bathurst to-day an English syndicate joined with a Canadian syndicate, who are in possession of the greatest iron ore deposit on the continent of America, who, in a few weeks, perhaps in a few days, will commence the building of a railway from the mines to the Intercolonial at Bathurst, who will make a complete investigation of the mine and who will ship their product to different points along the Intercolonial Railway system which will not only be of immense benefit to the Intercolonial Railway but which will afford our population the means of living in comfort, as they should live in a great country like this. We should have comfort, sir, we should have a population which can find employment at home instead of going away every year to seek work. The enterprise of the people will be stimulated

because immense industries will be established in connection with these ore deposits which will certainly be the equal of any other similar industries in Canada.
I claim, therefore, that the time has come when the government of Canada must devote its best thought and energy to the benefit of the people along the Intercolonial Railway, keeping in mind always that the Intercolonial is not operated for the benefit of the maritime provinces alone, but that it is operated for the direct benefit of the province of Ontario. While the construction of that road has brought comfort and a large measure of prosperity to the people of eastern Canada it has also brought riches and wealth to the farmers and manufacturers of Ontario. Therefore, I claim that the government must give its best thought to the question of improving the service of this great railway and we should expect from western Canada and from the province of Ontario that favourable consideration to which I think this project is entitled. The Intercolonial Railway has been looked upon more favourably recently than in years gone by. As my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmer-son) has said, we do not expect the government to rush into the acquisition of these branch lines, but as soon as the financial conditions permit we say that it would be a wise policy to undertake. But first of all the government must look into the conditions with respect to these branches. I am prepared to admit that perhaps some of them would not appeal at first sight to the judgment of a railway expert. If I remember aright the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, at the last session of parliament, said that if he were the president of a corporation having control of the Intercolonial Railway, he would first of all try to take in such branches as, in his judgment, it would be to the advantage of the Intercolonial to secure. Let him adopt this policy to-day or as soon as the financial condition of the country will permit. I have in my county not four branches, as my good friend from Kings and Albert (Mr. McAlister) has; I have only one branch, but permit me to say that it is certainly the very best branch of any connected with the Intercolonialother sources of the lumber industry, of the grindstone quarries and of the iron mining industry which is bound to be one of the greatest industries in the Dominion of Canada.
Hear, hear.

I am serious when I say so, Mr. Speaker, because it is well known that we have from Bathurst to Caraquet, Shippegan and Tracadie, a population of over 20,000 souls and it is among that population that we find the Gloucester fishermen who annually bring, upon the coast of that district, traffic to the Intercolonial Railway in the form of $1,500,000 worth of fish, taken from the bottom of the sea to be added to the 70i

At this late hour I shall not intrude for long on the patience of the House. Let me first of all extend my very hearty congratulations to the mover of this resolution (Mr. Emmerson) who supported his proposition by such a very logical and very eloquent speech. It gives me very great pleasure to endorse everything the hon. gentleman has said on this subject with which he is so familiar. In his opening remarks he carried us back to the days when the people of the maritime provinces were dealing with the New England states, and I can recollect very well that when I started housekeeping myself in the town of Chatham my furniture was bought in the city of Boston and brought around by schooner. Compare the conditions of trade in those days with the conditions of to-day and what a vast difference you will find. Instead of the merchandise which we use coming from the New England states it comes from Ontario and Quebec, to the great advantages of the industries in these manufacturing provinces. I agree also with what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) said, that if there be low rates on the Intercolonial Railway, it is not only the consuming population of the maritime provinces that enjoys the benefit, but that benefit is shared in by the producers of Ontario, so that there is a mutual advantage. I wish to place myself on record as being in favour of this resolution, and I endorse very strongly the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Guysbor-ough (Mr. Sinclair) who was not only in favour of taking over and operating the branch lines but who was in favour of developing those parts of the maritime provinces which have no railways and which if they had would contribute greatly to the traffic on the Intercolonial. I want specially to point out that there are two sections in my county which have been settled for 100 years and which would be splendid freight producing sections but which are still without any railway facilities whatever. I ask the Minister of Railways to bear in mind the petition that has been in his department for some time asking the government to fayourablv consider the extending of a branch line from a point near the town of Newcastle to Tabusintac. It is well known
to every one who is acquainted with the Miramichi river that this is a very rich part of the country and that a very valuable catch of fish is taken at the lower end of the river, which is at present from 15 to 20 miles from any railway point. I wish also to draw the attention of the minister to another petition which has been in his

department for a long time, asking for the extension of the Intercolonial Railway from Indiantown to Red Bank, a distance of 8 miles across the peninsula, between the two branches of the main river where there is at present a large saw-mill and that portion of my county is a rich agricultural district. That district has also been settled for the last 100 years and they are still without railway facilities. I would point out that when you have these branch lines operated by the Intercolonial you can get the long haul on the freight. I might mention that there are 200 carloads of fish originating at the stations of Chatham and Loggieville, and when the Canada Eastern was owned by a private corporation this freight was hauled to Fredericton and then delivered to the Canadian Pacific Railway. But now, the Intercolonial Railway instead of carrying that freight at 10 cents per 100 pounds from Chatham to Fredericton, as was the case with the private corporation, they charge 13 cents per 100 for the same mileage and they have such control over the freight that if you do not give them the long haul they charge practically a local rate for the short haul. The consequence is that the freight originating at Chatham and Loggieville now goes round the long haul on the Intercolonial Railway instead of going to Fredericton and thence over the Canadian	Pacific Railway. This
simply illustrates that every branch railway has a great deal to do with the routing of the freight that originates on it. For example, on the Kent Northern Railway the freight that originates at Rexton and Richi-bucto will go to Kent Junction and thence to St. John whence it is handed over to the Canadian Pacific Railway, whereas if that branch was owned by the Intercolonial Railway and they could route the traffic originating on it they could divert it by way of Montreal and get the long haul. I heartily endorse what has been said by the mover of the resolution and I hope the day is not far distant when the financial conditions of the country will enable us to absorb and properly equip and maintain the branch lines as a portion of the Intercolonial, and to build such other branch lines not now in existence as will develop the traffic of that country and encourage industry and enterprise there.

As the hour is late I rise simply for the purpose of putting myself on record as approving of the statement contained in the resolution. As I understand that resolution it does not commit the government in any way to the purchase of these branch lines'; it simply means that where it is good business policy, where it is in the best interests of the country and the Intercolonial Railway to acquire these lines, the government [ Mr. LOGGIE.
should have the endorsation of parliament in pursuing such a course. And while I endorse the policy of acquiring the branch lines I think the more important policy is to extend the Intercolonial Railway to districts where the conditions will justify such extension. I have in my mind a case in point; I have photographs which I intend to show the Minister of Railways when the opportunity arises, and I think I can convince him that if we have not a Cobalt we have something nearly approaching it. I will, when the opportunity comes, press on the minister the advisability of building a branch line from Merigomish to Antigonish via Arisaig and thence to Country Harbour. Possibly I shall take the opportunity of bringing this matter up when the House is in committee of supply.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the very valuable discussion that has taken place to-night has been of interest to every member of the House, not only to those who come from the maritime provinces, but equally so to us who live in other parts of the Dominion. I would feel a little diffidence, even if I had the time, about discussing this question after the very eloquent and able address which has been delivered by my hon. friend from Westmoreland. He has given to this question a great deal of study. Indeed, sir, he has given to the greater question of transportation a study perhaps not equalled by that of any other man in this House; and the grasp of the situation which he has shown to-night proves that he has not rushed to his conclusions but has reached them after the most careful and I believe honest and candid consideration. Such discussions in this House must be of interest to all Canada. Possibly sometimes they do not accomplish the object which we are seeking at the moment; but they do diffuse a large amount of information which leads the people to take a broader view of the questions which interest us all. I was particularly struck with the broad view my hon friend took of the situation. While he did point out what conclusions could be drawn if we took the sectional view, he discouraged this, and spoke from the broader view of carrying all the products of the country from the point where they are produced to the point where they are consumed, which is of general interest to all Canada, and does not pertain to any particular section of the country. I did not rise to go into this question to-night. It is not a question that can be brushed aside lightly, but is one of great interest to the west as well as to the east. With the permission of my bon. friend, I will not make a statement on behalf of the government to-night, but when 1 make the speech on the "intercolonial which is customary on going into Supply,

I will make a statement as to the position of the government on this question and on all other questions relating to the Intercolonial Railway, I will therefore move the adjournment of the debate.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned
